answer: Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy for their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [1]. When doing so, they must consider their technical knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use, and the persons or groups on whom the AI systems are to be used [1].

Under the AI Act, prohibited AI practices include the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques [1]. The objective or effect of these techniques must be to materially distort the behaviour of a person or a group of persons by appreciably [1]. Additionally, AI systems used to detect the emotional state of individuals in situations related to the workplace and education should be prohibited [2].

According to the AI Act, an 'AI system' is defined as a machine-based system designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy, which may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment and which, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers from the input it receives how to achieve them [2].

answer: An AI system is considered high-risk if it is listed in Annex III [1, 5]. Additionally, an AI system is classified as high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Union harmonisation legislation and fulfills the conditions of Article 6 [2].

The risk-management system for high-risk AI systems should adopt the most appropriate risk-management measures in light of the state of the art in AI [1]. It should consist of a continuous, iterative process planned and run throughout the entire lifecycle of the system [2]. This process is aimed at identifying and mitigating relevant risks to health, safety, and fundamental rights [2]. Additionally, it should include identifying the possible risks arising from the interaction between the AI system and its operating environment, as well as reasonably foreseeable misuse [1].

High-risk AI systems that use techniques involving the training of AI models must be developed using training, validation, and testing data sets that meet specific quality criteria and are subject to data governance [1]. These data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, free of errors to the best extent possible, and complete in view of the intended purpose [5]. Additionally, they must possess the appropriate statistical properties, including regarding the persons or groups of persons in relation to whom the high-risk AI system is intended to be used [5].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.59 | eu_ai_act_20 p.20 | eu_ai_act_20 p.59
answer: High-risk AI systems must technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system [1, 2]. These logging capabilities must enable the recording of events relevant for identifying situations that may result in the system presenting a risk or a substantial modification, facilitating post-market monitoring, and monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems [1, 5]. Additionally, for high-risk AI systems referred to in point 1(a) of Annex III, the logging capabilities must provide at a minimum the recording of the period of each use, including the start and end date and time [5].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.60 | eu_ai_act_20 p.60 | eu_ai_act_20 p.21 | eu_ai_act_20 p.21 | eu_ai_act_20 p.60
answer: High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so that natural persons can effectively oversee them during their period of use, using appropriate human-machine interface tools [1]. Human oversight aims to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may emerge when the system is used as intended [1]. Natural persons assigned to human oversight should be enabled to understand the system's capacities and limitations, monitor its operation, detect anomalies, and remain aware of the tendency to over-rely on its output [2, 5]. High-risk systems should also include mechanisms to guide and inform the overseer to make informed decisions on when and how to intervene, or to stop the system if necessary [3]. Furthermore, appropriate human oversight measures must be identified by the provider before the system is placed on the market or put into service [4].

cited_pages: eu_ai_act_20 p.25 | eu_ai_act_20 p.67 | eu_ai_act_20 p.41
answer: Deployers of high-risk AI systems must take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use such systems in accordance with their accompanying instructions for use [2]. They play a critical role in ensuring the protection of fundamental rights, complementing the obligations of the provider [1]. Due to their precise knowledge of the context of use, deployers can identify potential significant risks that were not foreseen in the development phase [1]. Additionally, deployers, along with providers and other relevant parties, should also be encouraged to apply additional requirements on a voluntary basis, such as those related to the Union's Ethics Guidelines [4].
The deployer of the high-risk AI system must carry out the fundamental rights impact assessment prior to deploying the system [1, 5].

In cases involving the rights and freedoms of third parties, this transparency obligation is limited to disclosing the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display, enjoyment, or normal exploitation of the work, while maintaining its utility and quality [3].

In order for processing to be lawful, personal data should be processed on the basis of the data subject's consent or another legitimate basis laid down by law, either in the regulation or in other Union or Member State law [3]. Additionally, the processing of personal data strictly necessary for preventing fraud constitutes a legitimate interest of the data controller [1].

Yes, the data subject has the right to withdraw their consent at any time, and it must be as easy to withdraw consent as it is to give it [1, 4]. The withdrawal of consent does not affect the lawfulness of processing that was based on consent before its withdrawal [1, 4]. Regarding the conditions for consent, the request for consent must be presented in a manner that is clearly distinguishable from other matters, and in an intelligible, easily accessible form using clear and plain language [1]. Furthermore, prior to giving consent, the data subject must be informed thereof [4]. When assessing if consent is freely given, utmost account must be taken of whether the performance of a contract or a service is conditional on consent to processing personal data that is not necessary for that performance [4].

Under the GDPR, the processing of a child's personal data in relation to information society services is lawful where the child is at least 16 years old [1]. However, Member States may provide by law for a lower age, provided that this lower age is not below 13 years [4].

Under the right of access, the data subject has the right to obtain confirmation from the controller as to whether or not their personal data are being processed [1]. If that is the case, they are entitled to access the personal data and receive information regarding the purposes of the processing, the categories of personal data concerned, and the recipients or categories of recipients to whom the data have been or will be disclosed [1].

A data subject has the right to erasure ('right to be forgotten') when the retention of the personal data infringes the GDPR or Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject [1]. This right also applies when the personal data are no longer necessary for the purposes for which they were collected or otherwise processed, or when the data subject has withdrawn consent or objects to the processing [1, 2].

The right to data portability allows a data subject to receive the personal data concerning them, which they have provided to a controller, in a structured, commonly used, and machine-readable format [3, 4]. Additionally, data subjects have the right to have these personal data transmitted directly from one controller to another, where technically feasible [4]. This right applies when the processing is based on consent or a contract, but it does not apply to processing necessary for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest [1, 4].

A data subject has the right not to be subject to a decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling, which produces legal effects concerning them or similarly significantly affects them [1, 2]. Furthermore, they have the right to obtain meaningful information about the logic involved, as well as the significance and the envisaged consequences of such automated decision-making [4].

Data protection by design and by default involves measures such as minimising the processing of personal data, pseudonymising personal data as soon as possible, and ensuring transparency with regard to the functions and processing of personal data [1]. It also includes enabling the data subject to monitor data processing and enabling the controller to create and improve security features [1]. To implement this, the controller must take into account the state of the art, implementation costs, the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, and the risks to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [2]. These appropriate technical and organisational measures must be implemented both at the time of determining the means for processing and during the processing itself [2].

A personal data breach must be notified to the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after the controller has become aware of it [1, 3]. This requirement applies unless the breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [1, 3]. If the notification cannot be achieved within 72 hours, it must be accompanied by reasons for the delay [2].

A data protection impact assessment is required prior to processing in cases where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons [3]. Specifically, it is required for a systematic and extensive evaluation of personal aspects based on automated processing, including profiling, that produces legal effects or significantly affects the person [4]. It is also required for large-scale processing of special categories of data, biometric data, or data on criminal convictions, as well as for the monitoring of publicly accessible areas on a large scale, particularly using optic-electronic devices [1, 2]. Furthermore, it is required for operations where the competent supervisory authority considers the processing likely to result in a high risk because it prevents data subjects from exercising a right, using a service or contract, or is carried out systematically [1].

The controller and processor must designate a data protection officer in any case where the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except for courts acting in their judicial capacity) [4]. Additionally, a data protection officer must be designated when the core activities of the controller or processor consist of processing operations requiring regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale [4]. Furthermore, state law shall designate a data protection officer, and Member State law may also require controllers to consult with and obtain prior authorisation from the supervisory authority for specific tasks [1, 2].

Under the GDPR, certain infringements are subject to administrative fines of up to 20 000 000 EUR, or up to 4 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [4]. Additionally, infringements of other specified provisions are subject to administrative fines of up to 10 000 000 EUR, or up to 2 % of the total worldwide annual turnover of the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [5]. Furthermore, if a controller or processor infringes several provisions, the total amount of the fine shall not exceed the amount specified for the gravest infringement [5].

Entscheidungen mit Rechtswirkung dürfen gemäß Art. 22 Abs. 1 DS-GVO grundsätzlich nur von Menschen getroffen werden [2]. Ausnahmen von diesem Grundsatz sind nur in bestimmten Fällen zugelassen, wie beispielsweise bei einer Einwilligung der betroffenen Person [2].

Bei geschlossenen Systemen erfolgt die Datenverarbeitung in einer eingegrenzten und technisch abgeschlossenen Umgebung mit einem eng begrenzten Anwender:innenkreis [1]. Die Kontrolle über die Ein- und Ausgabedaten liegt hier bei den Anwendenden [1]. Offene Systeme werden hingegen beispielsweise als Cloud-Lösung betrieben und sind über das Internet für einen unbestimmten Anwender:innenkreis zugänglich [2]. Dabei verlassen die Eingabedaten den geschützten Bereich und können je nach Konzeption auch für das weitere Training oder die Beantwortung von Anfragen anderer Nutzer:innen verwendet werden [2].

Vor der Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten ist zunächst eine generelle Bewertung des Risikos hinsichtlich Art, Umfang, Zweck und Umständen vorzunehmen [1]. Wird dabei festgestellt, dass die Verarbeitung voraussichtlich ein hohes Risiko für die Rechte und Freiheiten natürlicher Personen zur Folge hat, ist eine Datenschutz-Folgenabschätzung (DSFA) nach Art. 35 DS-GVO erforderlich [2]. Beim Einsatz von KI-Anwendungen wird dies vielfach der Fall sein [2]. Darüber hinaus veröffentlichen die Datenschutzaufsichtsbehörden sogenannte „Muss-Listen“ zu Verarbeitungen, für die eine DSFA durchgeführt werden muss [2].
Beschäftigte sollten keine privaten Accounts und Geräte für KI-Anwendungen nutzen, da auf diese Weise Profile zu den jeweiligen Beschäftigten entstehen können [2].
